title: Integrated Drill-hole-sharing Strategy for Precise Double-step Sliding Genioplasty: A Standardized Digital Workflow.
abstract: Double-step sliding genioplasty is a potential surgical option for patients with severe chin retrusion who wish to avoid bilateral sagittal split ramus osteotomy (BSSRO). Compared with conventional single-step procedures, the double-step approach allows greater advancement, potentially improving chin projection and facial harmony in severe cases. However, this technique requires the execution of two precise, parallel osteotomy lines and the stable fixation of three separate bone segments. Such complexity is difficult to manage using traditional experience-based methods and manual plate bending, with a potential risk of unplanned segment rotation or displacement. This case report details a 31-year-old patient treated via a standardized digital workflow utilizing an integrated drill-hole-sharing strategy. To facilitate translation from virtual planning to surgical execution, a tooth- and bone-supported hybrid osteotomy guide and a patient-specific Ti-6Al-4V plate were co-designed within a single coordinate system. This co-design aligns each predrilled channel with its corresponding plate hole after planned segment repositioning. Intraoperatively, the guide localized the osteotomy lines and established seven predrilled channels. Following osteotomy, the patient-specific plate functioned as a reduction device. By progressively inserting screws into the shared channels, controlled traction was generated to guide the multiple bone segments into their planned three-dimensional positions, thereby minimizing repeated trial fitting and preserving more bone tissue. Exploratory postoperative assessment showed close agreement between the planned and achieved positions in this case. At 1 month, three-dimensional deviations were 0.50 and 0.28 mm at the intermediate and distal segment drill-hole midpoints, respectively, and 0.19, 0.37, and 0.51 mm at pogonion, gnathion, and menton. Postoperative soft-tissue changes included a labiomental angle change from 142.56° to 120.67° and 9.47 mm soft-tissue pogonion advancement. These exploratory findings suggest that the integrated workflow may facilitate the transfer of virtual planning to complex multi-segment chin repositioning, although its accuracy and operative efficiency require further comparative validation.

title: The evolutionary role of dance: Group bonding but not prosocial altruism.
abstract: That synchronized activities like dancing or marching positively influence social bonding has been widely demonstrated for both dyads and small groups. However, previous studies of other social bonding behaviors (laughter and behavioral synchrony) have suggested that these prosocial effects do not extend to altruistic actions (generosity in economic games), implying that social bonding and prosociality may be underpinned by different psychological processes. Here, we ask whether dancing to music in a naturalistic (i.e., nonlaboratory) context makes people feel more socially bonded and/or more altruistic (in an economic game) compared to another real-world, exertive activity (group-based gym circuit training sessions).We found that the type of activity did not affect measures of either social bonding or generosity.However, confirming the earlier findings for laughter, we showthat while any form of exertive activity elevates the sense of group bonding (entitativity), it has no effect either on ratings of willingness to act prosocially toward another individual, or on actually acting generously toward them in an economic game. Taken together, these results suggest that altruism, cooperation, and other forms of prosociality may be the outcome of creating bonded relationships and groups, rather than their cause.

title: Social Pressure and Prosocial Behaviors Among Teenagers
abstract: This study investigates the influence of social pressure on prosocial behaviors among adolescents through a lab-in-the-field experiment. Using a controlled environment where teenagers interact with their classmates, I examine the evolution of cooperation over repeated interactions and explore its determinants. I find that girls and altruistic pupils demonstrate higher levels of cooperation. The introduction of non-monetary rewards and punishments, serving as forms of social pressure, significantly enhances cooperation among adolescents, aligning their behavior with group's cooperation. Surprisingly, the study finds that the intensity of social pressure does not directly impact cooperation, suggesting that adolescents adapt their pro-social behavior in response to social pressure awareness. This study demonstrates that peer-enforced norms sustain cooperation among adolescents, even in the absence of material incentives.

title: Perceived Clinical Utility of a Routine Family Experience Feedback Loop in Pediatric Palliative Care.
abstract: Home is typically the preferred setting of care for children living with serious illness, yet children and families frequently experience unmet needs in the home. Pediatric palliative care (PPC) teams provide longitudinal support for these children and families but have limited insight into families' day-to-day experiences and needs while at home. Routinely collecting family-reported data about care experiences in the home and sharing these data with PPC teams may enable more timely, responsive, and family-centered care. To evaluate the perceived clinical utility of sharing routinely collected, digitally enabled, family-reported data between families and PPC teams. We used a modified experience-based co-design approach to evaluate acceptability, perceived feasibility, and perceived clinical actionability through 1) individual interviews with family participants, (2) "clinical action check-in" meetings with outpatient PPC clinicians, and (3) co-design sessions with PPC and hospice clinicians. We used a content analytic approach to identify codes, categories, and themes. Twenty-four parents of children with serious illness and 11 PPC and hospice clinicians participated in this project. Sharing routinely collected care experience data was perceived as: (1) acceptable or valuable, although comfort and willingness varied for families, (2) feasible with attention to timing, frequency, recipients, and implementation, and (3) clinically actionable along a spectrum. A routinely collected, digitally enabled feedback loop between home and hospital is perceived by families and clinicians as holding promise for helping teams identify unmet needs and tailor care. Facilitating routine, bidirectional communication between families and teams may improve alignment between the care provided and families' needs at home.

title: Peers link conflict-resolution reputation to social and cognitive capacities rather than the capacity to impose costs among Ethiopian forager-horticulturalists
abstract: Leadership emergence in socially egalitarian contexts depends on the qualities of individuals and on how others perceive their capacity to use them. Multi-Capital Leadership theory proposes that leaders deploy material, social, somatic, and neural capital to solve problems of group living by providing benefits to group members or imposing costs. Conflict resolution is one important leadership domain. We reanalyse peer rankings of 60 adults in a relatively egalitarian community of Chabu forager-horticulturalists in southwest Ethiopia. Seven peer-raters ranked participants on twelve traits identified as relevant to leadership in contemporary evolutionary theories. A previous analysis averaged rankings before modelling, obscuring differences among raters and treating positions within an ordering as continuous measurements. Here, we fitted a multivariate Plackett–Luce model directly to the individual rankings. This accounts for dependence within rankings and incorporates uncertainty into estimates. It also allows us to estimate consensus orderings and systematic variation associated with rater sex. Male and female peer-raters produced broadly similar orderings, including for conflict resolution. This could reflect actual covariation in participants’ qualities, a shared evaluative schema, or both. Peer-ranked proxies for material, social, and neural capital covaried closely and did not form clearly separable perceptual domains. The clearest descriptive contrast was between benefit-related attributes, including conflict resolution, sound decision-making, and prosociality, and cost-related attributes, including being feared and fighting. Conflict-resolution reputation was most closely associated with decision-making, kin support, respect, and intelligence, and showed no clear positive association with fighting. In these rankings, a reputation for conflict resolution was more clearly distinguished from aggression and coercion than were measures capturing the three capital domains represented in the instrument.

title: Ryan House: Sharing 15 Years of Inpatient Pediatric Respite and Hospice Experience.
abstract: BackgroundA 2021 UNICEF report estimates that nearly 240 million children live with disabilities globally, including children with medical complexity (CMC). In the United States, over 2 million children have complex medical needs requiring around-the-clock care, creating significant physical, emotional, and financial burdens for their families.ObjectiveTo describe the organizational structure, financial support, medical staffing model, and patient demographics of Ryan House, aiming to establish its framework as a global standard that can be adapted to support communities worldwide.Setting & InterventionRyan House is one of only 3 inpatient pediatric facilities in the United States offering dedicated respite and palliative hospice services for CMC. The facility provides a flexible, community-based care model designed to extend support from clinical settings into the home life of families.ResultsDuring its 15 years of operation, Ryan House has served over 1100 patients and families, delivering more than 24 000 days of care. The manuscript details the specific operational, staffing, and funding structures that enabled this level of service delivery.ConclusionRyan House represents a unique and critical resource for families caring for CMC. Its operational model offers a scalable and adaptable framework that can be implemented globally to alleviate caregiving burdens and improve quality of life for complex pediatric populations.

title: Cooperative and competitive interactions modulate expectations about resource distribution in 13-month-old infants
abstract: Cooperation and resource distribution are central properties of human sociality. The long-term stability of cooperative ventures depends on linking obtained benefits to the efforts invested by collaborating partners. Previous studies demonstrated that infants start to both understand and engage in cooperative activities early on and show early sensitivity to how resources are distributed among social partners. It remains unknown, however, whether infants' intuitions about expectable resource sharing are influenced by the cooperative or competitive nature of the social partners' preceding interactions. We examined this issue by presenting 192 thirteen-month-old infants with various “predator-prey” chasing events in which two goal-directed agents interacted either cooperatively or competitively to capture a chasee. Using a violation-of-expectation looking-time paradigm we tested infants' expectations about different patterns of resource distribution (involving sharing vs. monopolizing) the agents engaged in after capturing the prey. Following familiarization to Cooperative Chasing interactions infants looked significantly longer when the obtained goal outcome was consumed by one of the chasers alone than when it was shared. In contrast, after observing Competitive Chasing events infants showed the opposite pattern of expectations looking longer when the captured prey was shared by the two chasers than when one of them consumed it on its own. Together with the control conditions, these findings suggest that 13-month-olds use the cooperative versus competitive structure of a preceding interaction to generate expectations regarding the sharing or monopolization of the obtained resource.

title: Strengthening older adults' healthcare reform in Nigeria through policy analysis and lessons from participatory health system innovations in Africa.
abstract: Nigeria has expanded its policy architecture for ageing, yet older adults continue to face fragmented services, weak financial protection, limited age responsive care, and substantial barriers to healthcare access. This study examined why increasing policy recognition has not translated consistently into implementation and whether participatory health system innovations elsewhere in Africa offer relevant lessons for reform. A desk-based policy analysis was undertaken using Walt and Gilson's Health Policy Triangle to examine the context, actors, content, and process shaping older adults' healthcare in Nigeria. Purposively identified legislation, policy documents, institutional reports, and peer reviewed literature were interpreted deductively across the four HPT domains, with particular attention to five major national legislative and policy developments enacted or approved between 2004 and 2022. Comparative evidence from Zimbabwe's Friendship Bench, South Africa's older adult peer support model, Ghana's Community Based Health Planning and Services programme, and Rwanda's community health worker system was examined for potentially transferable principles rather than models for direct replication. The analysis identified an implementation gap arising from interacting constraints across all four policy domains. Demographic and epidemiological pressures are increasing within a resource constrained health system; institutional responsibilities remain fragmented; older adults and caregivers have limited influence in health governance; and broad policy commitments are not consistently matched by operational provisions for long term care, age responsive primary healthcare, workforce development, financing, monitoring, and accountability. The comparative cases highlighted potentially relevant principles including community participation, task sharing, peer support, integration with primary healthcare, structured supervision, and stronger referral pathways. However, the evidence base is heterogeneous: only some interventions were designed specifically for older adults, and differences in governance, financing, workforce capacity, and health system organisation constrain direct transferability. Strengthening older adults' healthcare in Nigeria therefore requires greater attention to implementation rather than additional policy commitments alone. Reform should strengthen coordination, financial protection, age disaggregated monitoring, meaningful participation, and integration of community-based approaches within existing health system structures. Comparative innovations should be contextually adapted and evaluated through phased implementation before wider scale up.

title: Game structure shapes normative preferences and inter-brain neural synchrony in free-allocation public goods games
abstract: Threshold public goods games (TPGGs) are generally expected to facilitate coordination more effectively than linear public goods games (LPGGs), because an explicit provision point can support non-zero equilibria and transform a social dilemma into a coordination problem. This prediction, however, is based largely on settings in which group members contribute to a single shared pool. Whether it extends to environments in which individuals freely allocate resources across multiple partners remains unknown. Here, using a three-person ring network and functional near-infrared spectroscopy hyperscanning, we examined how free allocation shaped behavioral and neural signatures in the two game structures. Contrary to conventional expectations, the LPGG produced stronger partner-specific reciprocity and greater alignment to history-dependent contribution standards than the TPGG. This behavioral differentiation was accompanied by stronger dyadic inter-brain synchrony in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex during the LPGG. The two structures also elicited distinct patterns of individual neural activity and dmPFC–rTPJ functional connectivity. These findings suggest that the expected coordination advantage of threshold public goods games may not generalize to settings that allow partner-specific resource allocation, highlighting the importance of allocation flexibility in shaping the relationship between game structure and cooperative behavior.

title: The sense of responsibility and bystanders’ prosocial behavior in cyberbullying: The mediating role of compassion and the moderating roles of moral outrage and moral disgust
abstract: The sense of responsibility can play an important role in the behavior of college students involved in cyberbullying incidents. Research on the relationship between the sense of responsibility and bystander behavior in cyberbullying is limited. This study examined the relationship between the sense of responsibility and prosocial cyberbystander behavior in cyberbullying, focusing on investigating compassion as a mediator and moral emotions (i.e., moral outrage and moral disgust) as a moderator in this relation. A total of 1,114 Chinese college students (35.4% female), aged from 18 to 23 years (M = 19.55, SD = 1.05), completed an online questionnaire. Results showed that compassion played a partial mediating role in the relationship between the sense of responsibility and prosocial cyberbystander behavior. Moral outrage moderated the relationship between the sense of responsibility and prosocial cyberbystander behavior. Specifically, among participants with higher levels of moral outrage, the relationships between the sense of responsibility and prosocial cyberbystander behavior became much weaker. These results provide a new direction for promoting prosocial cyberbystander behavior.

title: Vigilance decrement with upright and inverted faces.
abstract: The vigilance decrement is a decline in performance that occurs when people monitor infrequent and unpredictable signals for a sustained period of time. Prior studies measured vigilance for sensory stimuli (e.g., intensity) and cognitive stimuli (e.g., letters) but not for social stimuli. The current study determined whether the vigilance decrement occurs with faces, and whether the decrement depends on facial orientation. We expected the vigilance decrement to occur with inverted faces because they are more difficult to recognize and remember (i.e., the face inversion effect) and thus presumably deplete cognitive resources. Participants monitored inverted or upright faces for 40 min and we measured hits and false alarms, response time, sensitivity, response bias, task workload, and stress. As expected, the vigilance decrement occurred with inverted faces. Unexpectedly, it also occurred with upright faces. A possible explanation is that both vigilance and upright face perception share neural resources. Results were inconclusive regarding an effect of face orientation on the magnitude of the decrement. Future research is warranted to evaluate task-difficulty and resource-sharing accounts of the vigilance decrement in inverted and upright faces.

title: Social evaluation and decision-making in nonhuman primates
abstract: One of the challenges of living in a group is constantly having to decide when, how, and whom to interact with among several conspecifics in plenty of different contexts. For optimal decision-making, social animals can benefit from acquiring social information about others to selectively choose the most optimal partners to interact with. Accumulating research evidence that nonhuman primates form social knowledge and adapt their behaviours towards conspecifics that can benefit them. For example, individuals prefer interacting with the most cooperative and helpful group members, or the most competent at foraging tasks. Yet, how nonhuman primates acquire and use social information about others remains unclear. Their behaviours can be explained by an outcome-based process, associative learning strategies from past interactions, or by social evaluation inferences, impression formation about others from their past behaviours. In this thesis, I investigate whether nonhuman primates evaluate others’ characteristics and use their impressions to select social partners strategically. Three studies using different experimental settings were conducted on captive groups of Tonkean macaques (Macaca tonkeana) and brown capuchins (Sapajus apella) at the Centre de Primatologie – Silabe de l’Université de Strasbourg, in France. Both species live in multi-male, multi-female tolerant groups and have demonstrated selective partner choices, social knowledge, and cognitive skills. I first investigated whether Tonkean macaques and brown capuchins can evaluate the skilfulness of others and use their evaluation to select the optimal partner in two different contexts. In the first experiment, the subjects observed two human actors (skilful vs unskilled) trying to open several containers to release food. Afterward, Tonkean macaques and brown capuchins did not choose the skilful actor more frequently than the unskilled one to manipulate a food container. However, when their initial preferences for the actors were considered, the subjects successfully shifted their preference for the skilful actor – the better option to maximise reward outcomes. They did not learn to choose the skilful actor through direct experience during the test session nor did they base their decisions on the outcome they experienced in previous trials. Subjects also decreased their time looking at the unskilled actor after the demonstrations. Therefore, Tonkean macaques and brown capuchins used information about the actors’ skills to adapt their behaviours for optimising their food intake. Yet, as subjects experienced a differential reward after the actors’ demonstrations, an outcome-based process underlying their behaviours during the test cannot be ruled out. In contrast, for the second experiment, Tonkean macaques only observed two human actors (skilful vs unskilled) operating a puzzle task without obtaining food after the actors’ demonstrations. I then measured their probability of choosing the skilful actor – the optimal choice – to cooperate in a co-action version of the puzzle tasks. Tonkean macaques did not prefer to cooperate with the skilful over the unskilled partner. They did not spontaneously use information about the actors’ skills acquired by observation, nor did they learn through trials to use information from direct experience with the partners. Although recruiting a partner in a cooperative context might be more complex than the testing conditions in the first study, these results indicate that Tonkean macaques did not adapt their behaviours when direct experience with the partners during the demonstration phase was no longer possible. In a third experiment, I investigate whether Tonkean macaques can evaluate and prefer social agents that help rather than hinder others. For comparative purposes, I used a paradigm widely used to study children’s preference for helpers: the hill paradigm. Bonobos tested with the hill paradigm preferred hinderers over helper agents, contrasting previous findings on other nonhuman primates. Tonkean macaques watched several times videos in which an animated helper agent pushed a climber up a hill while an animated hinderer agent pushed the climber down the hill. No food was involved in the interactions between the animated agents, nor obtained by the subjects after the agents’ actions. Afterward, Tonkean macaques did not prefer the helper over the hinderer (or vice versa). No potential effects of perceptual features of the animated agents (shape, colour, movement) were found. While Tonkean macaques and bonobos share some behavioural and social characteristics, they do not show the same pattern of choices. Yet, the low level of attention of the subjects to the videos indicates a lack of interest in the experimental stimuli, raising a potential limitation of using videos and animated agents for testing this species. In conclusion, Tonkean macaques and brown capuchins used social information about the actors’ skills to inform their decisions, which supports previous findings that nonhuman primates can assess others’ competence. The results of the third study are however inconclusive to evidence an assessment of others’ prosocial tendencies in Tonkean macaques, in contrast to previous findings on other primate species. In addition, the findings do not evidence social reasoning skills corresponding to social evaluation inferences in these species and rather suggest that an outcome-based process underlies social information acquisition and decision-making in nonhuman primates. Yet, the inter-individual variation combined with the small sample sizes and potential methodological limitations found in this thesis call for further investigation of social evaluation in primates. Importantly, future studies using various experimental paradigms reflecting the species’ socio-ecological conditions are needed to better understand in which contexts evaluating and considering others’ competence or prosocial tendencies is valuable for each species.

title: Violence Prevention Climate in Korean Hospitals: Associations With Nurses' Workplace Violence Experiences and Organizational Citizenship Behavior.
abstract: To translate and validate the Violence Prevention Climate Scale for Korean nurses and to examine its associations with nurses' workplace violence by perpetrator and organizational citizenship behavior. Workplace violence is common in hospitals and harms nurses' well-being, work attitudes, and the quality and safety of care. Organizational attention to everyday practices, clear policies and procedures, and the reduction of pressure to ignore safeguards may lower violence and support prosocial behavior at work. This cross-sectional descriptive study involved a translation and content validation of the Violence Prevention Climate Scale, followed by an online survey of 965 Korean hospital nurses. Confirmatory factor analysis showed mixed fit for the theoretically specified three-factor model, and Cronbach's alpha values ranged from 0.86 to 0.92. When the three subdomains were modeled together, Pressure for Unsafe Practices was the only subdomain consistently associated with more violence across all perpetrator groups. Practices and Response was uniquely associated with lower odds of physician-initiated violence, whereas Policies and Procedures was uniquely associated with lower odds of nurse-to-nurse aggression. Practices and Response and Policies and Procedures were associated with higher organizational citizenship behavior in models without and with covariates. The small positive association between Pressure for Unsafe Practices and organizational citizenship behavior was statistically significant without covariates but not after covariate adjustment. The Korean version of the Violence Prevention Climate Scale showed promising evidence of validity and reliability for assessing organizational violence prevention efforts among Korean nurses, although structural validity requires further confirmation. Strengthening the violence prevention climate may help reduce workplace violence and promote prosocial behavior that supports high-quality care. Leaders should reduce workload and time pressures that can lead to safety shortcuts, ensure accessible reporting and timely visible responses to incidents, and maintain clear policies, education, and communication. The K-VPCS may guide diagnosis and targeted resource allocation to build safer and more respectful workplaces.

title: Advancing prosociality in extended reality: systematic review of the use of embodied virtual agents to trigger prosocial behaviour in extended reality
abstract: Attention has increasingly been focused on the potential of Extended Reality (XR) and Embodied Virtual Agents (EVAs) to significantly influence human behaviour. While an expanding body of literature explores the individual impacts of XR and EVAs, there is a noticeable gap in the literature regarding their combined influence on eliciting prosocial behaviour in humans. The purpose of this systematic review is to explore this intersection, offering insights into their multifaceted effects on human prosocial behaviour and the implications for future research and development of EVAs in XR. Our systematic review adopted a scoping approach due to the limited number of studies directly focused on EVAs (i.e., autonomously computer-controlled entities). Despite this, we observed the use of various forms of virtual characters (VCs) to elicit prosocial behaviour. An in-depth analysis of 15 selected studies indicates complex patterns in how XR and VCs affect users’ prosocial behaviour and interactions. Our review suggests that there is promising potential for EVAs to promote prosocial behaviour. However, further research is necessary to identify the design and interaction-related attributes that enhance the effectiveness of these technologies, particularly for socially interactive EVAs in XR environments.

title: JUMP Cell Painting chemical dataset: Morphological map of 115,796 compounds in human cells.
abstract: Image-based profiling decodes complex cellular states for high-impact biological and therapeutic applications, yet a large, public reference dataset of chemical perturbations has been lacking. We present Cell Painting images and 1.53 billion single-cell profiles for 115,796 compounds in human osteosarcoma cells, generated by the Joint Undertaking for Morphological Profiling (JUMP)-Cell Painting Consortium of 18 industry and non-profit partners. Despite technical variability across 12 data-generating laboratories, more than 15% of compounds show statistically significant phenotypic activity, reproducibility drops only 34% versus single-laboratory data, and compounds sharing biological targets often show similar image-based profiles. JUMP establishes a validated public reference resource that brings image-based profiling on par with genomics and transcriptomics. The dataset, shared alongside previously released genetic perturbation data in the Cell Painting Gallery, is a powerful predictive engine for the impact, mechanism, targets and activities of compounds, fundamentally accelerating chemical and cell biology and early-stage drug development.

title: Understanding health behaviors and resilience during pandemics: a systematic review of ethical, cognitive, and existential dimensions.
abstract: Pandemic events such as HIV/AIDS and COVID-19 destabilize not only public health systems but also the philosophical and ethical frameworks through which individuals interpret illness. Health behavior influenced by contagion challenges definitions of identity, perceptions of truth, moral reasoning, and core bioethical principles, including autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. This study employs a triadic lens, such as ontology, epistemology, and axiology, to examine how pandemic crises transform embodied experience, cognition, ethical response, and value-laden behavioral choices. From there, the consequences for health behavior are analyzed within both phenomenological and bioethical domains. Using a phenomenological framework, the study draws on interdisciplinary data, including clinical case reports, psychosocial literature, and first-person narratives. Philosophical constructs from Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, and Carel inform the mapping of existential vulnerability, cognitive distortion, and value formation. Bioethical principles from Beauchamp and Childress guide the interpretation of moral tensions arising in pandemic behavior, while public health ethics frameworks (e.g., Kass) contextualize collective obligations. Psychiatric presentations during COVID-19 provide illustrative grounding for abstract principles. Motivations and frameworks for pandemic health behaviors are reported as outcomes. A review of 134 articles helped frame the cognitive and ethical terrain of pandemic prevention and dissemination. Pandemics cause overlapping disruptions across ontological, epistemological, axiological, and bioethical levels. Embodied identity becomes fragmented by diagnostic classification, social distancing, and existential uncertainty, raising tensions between autonomy and relationality. Cognitive processing is hindered by emotional stress, misinformation, and isolation, leading to distorted perceptions of truth and reduced rationality, which complicates beneficent and non-maleficent decision-making. Moral behavior reflects value-based tensions-altruism, denial, concealment, stigma-negotiated within shifting contexts of personal risk, communal obligation, and distributive justice. These patterns illustrate how existential dislocation, epistemic fragmentation, and moral ambiguity shape lived experience and ethical behavior during a pandemic. Phenomenology offers vital insights into the human impact of pandemics by examining how relational, cognitive, and ethical dimensions shape illness experiences and health behaviors. Integrating bioethical principles clarifies why individuals struggle with autonomy, responsibility, and fairness during crises. To support recovery and coherence, public health governance must move beyond biomedical control toward emotionally attuned, ethically grounded care that emphasizes relational responsibility, moral imagination, and justice-oriented policy.

title: Preemptive solving of future problems: Multitask Preplay in humans and machines.
abstract: Humans can pursue a near-infinite variety of tasks, but typically can only pursue a small number at the same time. We hypothesize that humans leverage experience on one task to preemptively learn solutions to other tasks that were accessible but not pursued. We formalize this idea as "Multitask Preplay", an algorithm that replays experience on one task as the starting point for "preplay"-counterfactual simulation of an accessible but unpursued task. Preplay is used to learn a predictive representation that can support fast, adaptive task performance later on. When implemented within deep reinforcement learning, it predicts human generalization to novel tasks more accurately than traditional planning and predictive representation methods across grid-worlds and a 2D Minecraft domain. Additionally, Multitask Preplay improves an artificial agent's ability to generalize to new environments sharing task co-occurrence structure. These findings demonstrate that Multitask Preplay is a scalable theory of human counterfactual learning and generalization; endowing artificial agents with this capacity can significantly improve their performance in challenging multitask environments.

title: Receiving Social Support Motivates Long-Term Prosocial Behavior
abstract: Prosocial behavior—actions aimed to benefit other individuals, groups, or communities—are important for promoting and maintaining a healthy society. Extant research on the factors driving prosocial behavior has mainly addressed short-term effects, overlooking the factors that motivate long-term prosocial behavior. Building on attachment theory, we theorize that an interpersonal factor, receiving social support, can foster prosocial behavior in the long-term, both in the environment where the support was received and beyond it. We argue that receiving social support positively predicts felt security—a sense of being safe, cared for, and loved—which in turn associates with higher motivation to engage in behaviors that benefit others. We test our hypotheses with cross-sectional, longitudinal, retrospective, and experimental data. In Study 1, data from a sample of international business school alumni validate past research and show a significant positive relationship between receiving social support and engaging in prosocial behavior both within and beyond the environment in which support was received. Study 2 leverages data of US adults in a multi-wave study to show that receiving social support predicts prosocial activities several years later. Study 3 uses a retrospective survey to show that receiving social support relates positively to long-term prosocial behavior through higher felt security. Study 4 experimentally manipulates social support and further demonstrates that receiving social support fosters prosocial behavior through boosting felt security. Overall, our findings show that receiving social support motivates long-term prosociality through its positive association with felt security.

title: REMind: A Robot Role-Playing Game To Promote Bystander Intervention
abstract: Peer bullying is a pervasive social problem, with bystanders' inaction being a critical challenge despite widespread disapproval of bullying. Effective intervention strategies must move beyond explanation-based instruction to facilitate embodied situated learning. This dissertation explores how social robots can serve as mediators for applied drama to foster prosocial bystander intervention in the context of peer bullying. It introduces Robot-Mediated Applied Drama (RMAD): an innovative framework that integrates drama-based pedagogy with social robotics to create safe, reflective, and embodied learning experiences. Using a Research through Design (RtD) methodology, this work advances through an iterative sequence of design studies that culminate in the development and evaluation of REMind (short for Robots Empowering Minds): a mixed-reality role-playing game where children engage in dramatized bullying scenarios performed by social robots. In REMind, three robots enact a conflict involving a bully, a victim, and a passive bystander. Players are invited to assume control of robotic avatar, reflect on the unfolding narrative, and improvise an intervention by using the robot as a proxy in order to change the story’s outcome. Through this structure, children rehearse bystander intervention strategies within a psychologically safe, yet emotionally engaging environment. The iterative design process of REMind unfolded across complementary empirical inquiries. A crowdsourced feasibility study first established that observers perceive aggression toward robots as morally wrong, validating the viability of using robots in the intervention. A narrative co-design study with children revealed storytelling patterns such as preferences for emotionally expressive and customizable robot characters. Interviews with teachers grounded the design in classroom realities, identifying gaps in existing programs. A game design focus group study further examined what makes educational robot role-play games pleasurable for children, leading to identifying concrete design elements that informed REMind’s interactive components such as core mechanics, use of tangible props, world aesthetics and narrative structure. This dissertation presents the resulting artifact, REMind, as a system consisting of five interconnected components: Learning Goals, Mechanics, Narrative, Technology, and Aesthetics. The learning goals were defined through consultation with subject-matter experts to ensure grounding in evidence-based best practices. By deliberate aligning the game pleasures identified in prior studies with the learning objectives, REMind introduces a suite of game mechanics that scaffold socio-emotional skills (such as robot-mediated spect-actorship or "puppet mode" for moral intervention, interpretation of immersive affective displays for empathy-training and perspective taking, and custom-made logic-gate puzzles for moral reasoning). Narrative design is scaffolded by borrowing a five-step cognitive model of bystander intervention from social psychology. The technical implementation is realized through StorySync, a novel spreadsheet-based scripting toolkit developed to synchronize multimodal cues (including multiple robots, graphical interfaces, ambient lighting, and sound) and manage narrative branching for live interactive robot drama. Finally, the aesthetic elements leverages emotional design, ambient cues, and digital scenography to create an emotionally resonant learning experience. This concrete high-fidelity prototype serves as a proof of concept for RMAD. This research contributes a theoretical and practical foundation for designing robot-mediated experiential learning systems, offering RMAD as a new direction for social robotics and educational technology. It further illustrates how embodied storytelling and interactive systems design might cultivate reflective, prosocial action in a complex domain of social-emotional learning. More broadly, it advocates for a shift in Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) research toward systems thinking, positioning game design as a powerful systems lens for creating and analyzing holistic user experiences.

title: Psychological inoculation protects young women in South Africa against HIV prevention misinformation: Evidence from a randomised controlled trial.
abstract: Misinformation decreases public confidence in health technologies and willingness to use them. Psychological inoculation, or "prebunking", exposes people to misleading claims before they spread widely and refutes the claims and embedded persuasion tactics. Evidence on its effectiveness for HIV-related misinformation, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and among young women (a population highly vulnerable to HIV), is limited. We conducted a randomised controlled trial (July to October 2025) among 2,163 women aged 18-29 years recruited online in South Africa. Participants were randomly assigned to view two short TikTok-style inoculation videos addressing common myths about an HIV vaccine, or attention-matched control videos on nutrition and diabetes. All participants then viewed multiple false claims presented as social media posts. The primary outcome was intention to receive an HIV vaccine if available (1-10 scale), assessed immediately post-intervention and at three-week follow-up. Secondary outcomes included likelihood of recommending the vaccine; and perceived credibility, emotional impact, and shareability of misinformation claims. We used linear regression models to estimate intervention effects. Misinformation exposure reduced vaccine intentions by 0.63 points in the control group, while intentions increased by 0.30 points in the intervention group. Controlling for covariates and baseline intentions, post-exposure vaccine intentions were 0.92 points higher in the intervention group (95% CI 0.78, 1.06; p<0.01), a 12% relative increase. Intervention participants were also more likely to recommend the vaccine (+0.74; 95% CI 0.61, 0.88; p<0.01). Inoculation reduced perceived credibility, emotional distress, and sharing intentions across all false claims. Effects persisted at three-week follow-up (vaccine intentions: +0.97; 95% CI 0.78, 1.17; p<0.01). Brief, scalable psychological inoculation delivered via social-media-style videos protected young women's HIV vaccine intentions, with effects generalising to novel claims and persisting over three weeks. Prebunking campaigns may safeguard public confidence in other new HIV prevention technologies like lenacapavir.

abstract: Epigenetic regulation of gene expression plays a central role in brain plasticity during development and adulthood, and in response to the environment. While vertebrate models have provided important insights into these processes, systems that exhibit inducible and reversible plasticity throughout adulthood offer unique opportunities to investigate how environmental and social cues drive long-lasting changes in the brain, behavior, and physiology. title: Federated modular clinical decision support networks for collaborative learning in resource-limited settings.
abstract: Imperfect interoperability (IIO), where health facilities record different, often sparse subsets of clinical variables, remains a major barrier to deploying models trained with Federated Learning (FL) in global health settings. We introduce FedMoDN, a novel federated modular neural network architecture for collaborative learning across all features of an IIO distributed dataset, allowing healthcare facilities to use the full complement of their features without sharing, discarding, or imputing any data. We evaluate FedMoDN on a multi-site pediatric dataset comprising ~130,000 medical visits across 92 healthcare facilities in Tanzania and Rwanda. Across both internal and external validation health facilities, FedMoDN matches or surpasses models trained with centralized data sharing and competitive monolithic FL baselines, achieving a mean AUPRC of 0.80 versus 0.77 for the monolithic FL model on 18 external validation health facilities. Its relative advantage over a monolithic FL model rose from 4% (complete data) to 22% when 70% of test-time features were missing, and, unlike monolithic FL models, performance remained stable when health facilities contributed disjoint feature or label subsets. Furthermore, step-wise predictions provide clinically interpretable feature-attribution scores. By coupling IIO resilience with built-in interpretability, FedMoDN offers a promising decision support tool for resource-limited facilities sidelined by conventional FL.

title: How social norms emerge: the interindividual actor-critic
abstract: Social norms shape a vast range of human behaviors, from everyday interactions to major life choices. Yet, existing theories of norm emergence typically focus either on why certain norms arise (substantive properties) or on how they spread and persist (dynamical properties), often making conflicting assumptions. Here, we propose a unified account in which norms prescribing how one ought to act emerge naturally from the fundamental algorithms that guide individual learning—whether in social or non-social settings. Our account builds on recent advances in decision-making and emotion research that have highlighted ‘actor-critic’ models as a core mechanism of learning from feedback. We extend this mechanism to social settings by assuming that it is not only we who critique our actions, others critique our actions as well. By simulating this interindividual form of learning, we show that it uniquely produces group behavior that exhibits both substantive and dynamical properties of real-world social norms, including prosociality, ingroup bias, stickiness, S-shaped curves, and local conformity / global diversity. Our framework thus offers a uniquely parsimonious way to bridge the gap between individual learning and group behavior.

title: Linking Research Outputs to Support Transparency and Reproducibility in Preclinical Traumatic Brain Injury Studies: A Live Implementation Experience.
abstract: The PRE-Clinical Interagency reSearch resourcE-Traumatic Brain Injury (PRECISE-TBI) is a community-based consortium developing standards, resources, and tools to support preclinical traumatic brain injury (TBI) research. PRECISE-TBI aims to address barriers that contribute to the translational gap by improving transparency, interoperability, and accessibility of preclinical TBI data and methods. The PRECISE-TBI Education Focus Area develops and curates resources relevant to blast-related research, working with the broader community to address issues pertinent to both military and civilian populations. Using two complementary implementation examples, we illustrate the practical application of current PRECISE-TBI resources in preclinical TBI research, including the coordinated use of the Model Catalog and the Open Data Commons for TBI (ODC-TBI) repository. Together, these components form an integrated, FAIR-aligned publication and data sharing framework tailored to preclinical TBI research. We further describe a linked research output publication workflow, whereas traditional research articles are complemented by executable protocols hosted on protocols.io and curated, machine-readable datasets published as independent digital objects. This linked collection of research outputs has been referred to as the "Paper of the Future" in related PRECISE-TBI publications. These resources adhere to Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable principles through the use of persistent identifiers, rich metadata, and mapping to the community-defined Common Data Elements. This use case illustrates how PRECISE-TBI-aligned practices can facilitate compliance with the NIH Data Management and Sharing policy and provide a structured approach to documenting experimental design, provenance, and data limitations in preclinical TBI research. While this study does not evaluate downstream outcomes, the framework is intended to enable future assessment of data reuse, harmonization, and reproducibility by making research outputs transparent, citable, and evaluable through persistent cross-linking of publications, protocols, and datasets.

title: Optimal Detection of Selfish Nodes in Mobile Social Networks Through Improved Credit History and Fuzzy Game Theory Methodology
abstract: Mobile social networks include a self-organizing system consisting of several mobile wireless nodes. Node behavior due to selfishness can significantly reduce performance on mobile social networks. A selfish node intends to use its resources only for itself and is reluctant to share them with its neighbors. Therefore, identifying selfish nodes is essential to improve the performance of mobile social networks. This paper presents an improved method for optimal detection of selfish nodes, based on credit history and utilizing the information distribution method. The proposed method effectively recognizes selfish nodes and increases the cooperative motivation between network nodes. Among the various models, the fuzzy game theory model used to encourage the cooperation of selfish nodes is more efficient, and about 98.5% of the packets have reached their destination on time, which, in terms of energy consumption, delivery time, and best use of the intermediate nodes, outperforms other methods. If several intermediate nodes were willing to send packets, the node with the best conditions, which provided superior parameters and resources in exchange for an appropriate reward, was selected based on the importance of timely sending and minimizing energy consumption. The remaining approximately 1.5% of the transmitted packets were not successfully delivered.

title: Prosocial acts of influencers: The role of Vicarious Altruism on goal fulfilment in Green and Virtual Influencers
abstract: Prior research has indicated that green and virtual influencers play a significant role in promoting prosocial behavior in digital environments. Observing altruistic acts can evoke emotional reactions and inspire similar behaviors in others. Although previous research has highlighted the significance of emotions, authenticity, and clear communication, the specific processes that lead to vicarious altruism where individuals feel driven to act after witnessing altruistic behavior remain largely unexamined. To fill this gap, the current study utilizes a qualitative, exploratory approach, incorporating data triangulation. The findings reveal that content that emotionally resonates, is perceived as authentic, and includes relatable personal anecdotes significantly boosts prosocial behaviors, especially among young, educated women. In contrast, skepticism arises when messages appear insincere or misaligned with the influencer’s lifestyle. This study enhances the existing literature by applying the theory of vicarious altruism to the digital context, offering empirical insights into the emotional motivations driving online actions. It also provides practical recommendations for marketers and advocates of sustainability on how to create effective campaigns. Ultimately, the research highlights the critical role of authentic digital influence in nurturing emotional connection, ethical reflection, and impactful behavioral change.

title: Oxytocin restores context-specific hyperaltruistic preference
abstract: Recent advances in moral decision-making research show people are hyperaltruistic by being more willing to sacrifice monetary gains to spare others from suffering than to spare themselves. Yet other studies indicate an opposite egoistic bias: subjects are less willing to harm themselves for others' benefits than for their own. These results underscore the complexities of moral decisions and demand a mechanistic explanation for hyperaltruistic preferences. We investigated hyperaltruism using trade-off choices combining monetary gains and painful electric shocks and choices combining monetary losses and shocks. Study 1 revealed that switching the decision context from gains to losses effectively eliminated the hyperaltruistic preference, accompanied by the altered relationship between subjects' instrumental harm (IH) trait attitudes and relative pain sensitivities. In the pre-registered study 2, we found that oxytocin, a neuropeptide linked to parochial altruism, restored the context-dependent hyperaltruistic preference. Furthermore, oxytocin increased the degree to which subjects framed the task as harming others, which mediated the correlation between IH and relative pain sensitivities. Thus, the loss decision context and oxytocin diminished and restored the mediation effect of subjective harm framing, respectively. Our results help elucidate the psychological processes underpinning the contextual specificity of hyperaltruism and carry implications in promoting prosocial interactions.

title: Anatomical Interfaces as a Complementary Substrate for Structural MRI Representation in Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: Background Structural MRI analysis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) commonly relies on region-of-interest (ROI) summaries or voxel-level deep networks, neither of which explicitly quantifies the physical interfaces shared by adjacent brain regions. We investigated whether these anatomical interfaces provide structural information complementary to conventional regional measures. Methods T1-weighted MRI was segmented into 79 anatomical regions using a pretrained nnU-Net. Each region was represented as a graph node with six morpho-textural descriptors, while edges were defined only between regions sharing voxel-level face contact and characterized by Structural Contact and Boundary Appearance features. Results Correlation analyses showed generally limited redundancy between node- and interface-level descriptors, supporting partially distinct representational information. Node-controlled analyses further showed that selected interface features remained significantly associated with disease stage after adjustment for the morpho-textural characteristics of both connected regions, indicating that interface-level variation was not fully reducible to regional abnormalities. White matter hypointensity interfaces repeatedly emerged among the retained stage-associated effects. Selected Structural Contact features also showed convergent associations with clinical severity across CDR-SB, ADAS-Cog13, and MMSE. Representation ablation demonstrated that disrupting anatomical adjacency or removing interface attributes reduced classification performance, supporting the contribution of anatomically organized relational information. The full representation also improved multi-class classification relative to conventional ROI-vector and voxel-level baselines, with this advantage preserved on the independent NACC cohort without fine-tuning. Conclusions These findings indicate that anatomical interfaces provide measurable and complementary structural information beyond conventional region-wise morphometry, offering an interpretable framework for representing inter-regional structural relationships in neurodegenerative disease.

title: Language AI enables endogenous topic discovery and behavioral prediction from trust game perceptions
abstract: The Trust Game (and its many variants) is a widely used experimental paradigm for studying trust and prosocial behavior, yet its interpretation remains debated. We demonstrate endogenous topic discovery and labeling via language AI as a scalable complement to traditional methods, uncovering semantic themes not commonly associated with the game. Using 1,124 subjects’ descriptions of Trust Game interactions from two studies, we show that social concerns emerge as key predictors of prosocial behavior, alongside trust-related language, even when the interaction is framed as a loan repayment. The pipeline converts unstructured responses into predictions of individual decisions: we train a cross-validated XGBoost–Random Forest ensemble that classifies prosocial and selfish behavior from topic features alone well above chance (AUC 0.73). Explicit language categorized as risk, gambling, investment, or game-theoretic themes was less informative in models predicting passing than language categorized as trust, teamwork, or involving moral self-image. These findings both validate and challenge conventional assumptions, highlighting the importance of social and moral language in managerial decision-making.

title: Beyond deficit narratives: religious practice, meaning, and resilience in a national sample of New Zealand Muslims
abstract: Religious minorities often endure hostility, yet longitudinal data tracking the consequences of such threats are scarce. We report findings from the Muslim Diversity Study (N = 667) housed within the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (N = 32,193). Our population-weighted analyses show that New Zealand Muslims exhibit a distinct and devout religious profile. Although no more likely than other New Zealanders to endorse general spirituality (61% vs 63%), New Zealand Muslims report far higher rates of belief in God (92% vs 40%) and dramatically more frequent engagement in costly religious practices, such as worship and prayer. Muslims also report markedly higher religious and ethnic discrimination, with differences concentrated in domains most plausibly linked to Muslim identity rather than age- or gender-based discrimination. At the same time, New Zealand Muslims show broadly comparable health and distress outcomes, with higher meaning in life, neighbourhood cohesion, and self-esteem, and a small trend towards lower generalized social support. These cross-sectional findings are descriptive and motivate the study's core longitudinal aim: to quantify pathways by which religious culture may help sustain resilience under adversity.

title: Cognitive Mechanism of Influence of Subjective Social Class on Prosocial Risky Behaviour
abstract: Prosocial risky behaviour (PRB) combines risk and prosociality, defined as risk‐taking for the benefit of others or society. Its differences across subjective social classes and underlying mechanisms are unclear. Study 1 ( n = 590) used a questionnaire to explore the relationship between subjective social class and PRB. Study 2 ( n = 120) manipulated subjective social class and set risk levels in prosocial risky dilemmas to examine causal relationships and boundary conditions. Study 3 ( n = 120) used cognitive computational modelling to clarify effects and explore cognitive mechanisms. Results showed the following: (1) subjective social class negatively predicts PRB, especially in the 30%–50% risk range; (2) low social class individuals have lower loss aversion, higher guilt aversion and value PRB more; (3) two decision preferences parallel mediate the relationship between subjective social class and PRB. These findings offer insights for mitigating social class differences’ negative impacts and enhancing prosocial levels in risky situations.

title: Building a Culture of Safety Through Faculty Mentorship: The Peer Pairing Framework for Clinical Nurse Educators.
abstract: Clinical nurse educators often transition from bedside practice to clinical education in high-risk settings without structured support. Limited or absent mentorship during this transition may affect educator confidence, student learning outcomes, patient outcomes, and the ability to sustain a culture of safety. Although mentorship is widely recommended in nursing education, implementation strategies remain limited. The Peer Pairing Framework was developed as a staged mentorship approach to support clinical nurse educators and inform a comprehensive mentorship model. The Peer Pairing Framework was informed by a voluntary onboarding survey of 914 clinical faculty, of whom 73.52% expressed interest in having a mentor and 88% expressed interest in serving as mentors. Stage 1 paired experienced and novice clinical nurse educators in an academic quarter-long mentorship experience. A mixed-methods evaluation included 5 pre-and post-experience Likert-scale survey questions aligned with Certified Nurse Educator (CNE) and Academic Clinical Nurse Educator Certification (CNEcl) competencies, assessing 5 mentorship pillars: Retention/Intent to Stay, Sense of Community/Support, Competence, Confidence, and Growth/Engagement. Qualitative feedback was also collected. There were 53 participants representing 7 campuses that completed the mentorship experience. Participants completing the post-experience survey reported a mean score of 4.77 versus a baseline mean score of 4.35. The highest-rated domains were retention/intent to stay (5.00), confidence (5.00), and competence (4.86), while community/support (4.28) and professional growth (4.25) identified areas for improvement. Although statistical significance was not demonstrated, findings suggested there is potential for clinical significance. Further, qualitative findings highlighted peer support, professional connection, resource sharing, and role development for mentors and mentees. The Peer Pairing Framework represents a mentorship strategy designed to strengthen workforce safety by supporting clinical nurse educators during the transition into academia. Preliminary findings suggest that peer faculty mentorship may enhance retention, competence, confidence, and professional engagement while fostering a culture of safety in clinical learning environments. This staged approach offers a data-driven model for future comprehensive mentorship development.

title: Advancing FAIR sharing for epidemiological, clinical and public health study data: the German National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI4Health).
abstract: Access to high-quality, FAIR health data is essential for advancing epidemiological, public health and clinical research. NFDI4Health, one of the consortia of Germany's National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI), was established in 2020 to address this need by improving data FAIRness for the scientific community. During the initial funding phase, NFDI4Health developed key infrastructure components and services focusing on interoperability, data sharing and research support. Our approach was guided by user needs and real-world use cases in alignment with (inter)national FAIR standards and infrastructures. We advanced findability of health data by establishing a central Health Study Hub and connecting it to local infrastructures, e.g., through the Local Data Hub software, to facilitate transfer of metadata from the local infrastructures to the Health Study Hub. Accessibility was improved by expanding the German Research Data Portal for Health (FDPG) to provide central access to study data and by providing tools to support anonymisation and synthetic data generation. We also developed an interoperable metadata schema for publishing study data and implemented it in the Health Study Hub. To further improve interoperability, a NFDI4Health FAIR sharing collection and AI support for metadata annotation and harmonisation workflows were established. To enhance reusability, data quality assessment tools were further developed, and two frameworks for federated analysis of sensitive health data were piloted. Intensive engagement with our communities through training, advisory services, and collaborative development ensured user relevance. NFDI4Health has established a scalable, interoperable, and user-centred infrastructure to support FAIR data sharing in health research. Future work will focus on further developing and consolidating the infrastructure, expanding cross-domain data integration, fostering broader adoption within our research community, and strengthening national and international collaboration.

title: Ternary Moral Empathy Model from the Perspective of Intersubjective Phenomenology.
abstract: The phenomenon of empathy is an intersubjective process of feeling and a particular form of intentionality. Moral empathy refers to a type of empathy that can trigger moral action, with the embodied intersubjectivity laying the foundation for its emergence. This paper attempts to propose a comprehensive theoretical model of moral empathy from the perspective of intersubjective phenomenology, which includes the following. (1) The moral dimension of perceptual empathy: at the subpersonal, unconscious, and perceptual-motor level, embodied empathic practices are essential for the formation of moral consciousness and the emergence of moral empathy. (2) The moral dimension of situational empathy: following the development of shared attention mechanisms, children can direct towards the intentional objects of others through embodied situational cues to perceive the psychological state of others and generate the moral empathy of "ought", leading to dyadic morality that promotes cooperative behavior. (3) The moral dimension of narrative empathy: the narrative practices of moral empathy refer to the processes by which children could perceive and understand the moral situation of characters within an embodied narrative structure, subsequently generate prosocial motives such as empathic concern, and then accept the "objective" moral norms of the group consciousness embedded in the narrative.

title: Altered social-emotional processing and decision-making in Central Diabetes Insipidus: The role of vasopressin deficiency.
abstract: Arginine vasopressin (AVP) regulates homeostasis and social behavior. Damage to AVP neurons causes central diabetes insipidus (CDI), now termed arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D), a rare disorder potentially linked to social deficits. This study examined how AVP deficiency affects social, emotional, and psychological functioning in AVP-D patients. Twelve AVP-D patients and twelve matched controls participated. Blood samples measured copeptin and other hormones. Participants completed behavioral tasks assessing social exclusion (Cyberball paradigm), emotion recognition (Reading the Mind in Films), prosocial behavior (Social Discounting Task), fairness (Ultimatum Game), and approach-avoidance (Stop Distance Paradigm). Questionnaires assessed mood, anxiety, aggression, alexithymia, and empathy. Hormone analysis showed AVP-D patients had lower copeptin and lower ACTH levels. Psychometric tests indicated increased depression, aggression, and alexithymia. Both groups felt negative after social exclusion, but AVP-D patients adjusted less emotionally, showing smaller changes in insecurity and team spirit. AVP-D patients also struggled more with emotion recognition, linked to lower copeptin and higher alexithymia. Fairness sensitivity differences were minor and not significant. Both groups donated less as social distance grew, though AVP-D patients' decline was less steep. In approach-avoidance behavior, AVP-D patients kept greater distances from human faces with friendly or aggressive expressions, unlike with animal targets. AVP-D patients exhibit socioemotional impairments like poor emotion recognition and depression, highlighting the need for routine screening. Early detection enables targeted interventions, and addressing central AVP pathways is crucial, underscoring the need for treatments beyond hormone replacement.

title: Relationship Between Empathy and Prosocial Behavior
abstract: This study focused on the relationship between empathy and prosocial behavior among individuals aged between 18 to 30 years old . The sample consisted of 90 individuals, including both students and working professionals. The study used the Toronto Empathy Questionnaire (TEQ) to assess empathy and the Prosocialness Scale for Adults (PSA) was used to measure behavior with the aim of establishing if there exists a notable correlation, between these distinct factors. The study found a significant positive correlation (r = 0.847, p<.001) between empathy and prosocial behavior, suggesting that individuals with higher empathy are more likely to engage in prosocial acts. These results offer supporting evidence for establishing theories like the Empathy-Altruism Hypothesis and the Emotional Contagion Theory, which propose that empathy plays a crucial role in motivating altruistic behavior. According to the study, developing empathy in young people may improve prosocial behavior, resulting in more compassionate and socially responsible communities.

title: Group Selection Promotes Prosocial Prompts in Populations of LLM Agents
abstract: Current approaches to instill prosociality in large language model (LLM) agents often rely on humans specifying desired behaviors at the individual level, which does not guarantee cooperation within LLM populations. As frontier training shifts toward individual rewards for verifiable tasks, such as mathematics and coding, this outcome-based focus may further undermine cooperation in multi-agent settings. Large-scale cooperation in human populations emerged via unguided evolutionary mechanisms, not a central architect. Group selection, in which cooperative groups within a population outcompete less cooperative ones, has been argued to be essential. In this study, we explore whether group selection can promote cooperation in populations of LLM agents. We introduce a multi-agent simulation framework in which LLM agents play a repeated social dilemma game and transmit their natural-language prompts across generations under either individual- or group-level selection. Under group selection, prompts from high-performing groups are transmitted, thereby promoting prosociality and stabilizing cooperation. Under individual selection, self-interested prompts dominate, causing populations to collapse into collective defection. This gap is robust across prompt ablations, alternative game framings, and model swaps. We theoretically reproduce key results using a replicator-mutator model, whose empirical transmission kernel predicts a phase transition at a critical threshold. Preliminary findings show that, when informed about the selection mechanism, GPT-5.4 preemptively and gradually adjusts first-generation donations. This demonstrates strong anticipatory behavior that was not observed in the other tested models. These results demonstrate that prosocial prompts and cooperative behaviors evolve in LLM agent populations under group selection.

title: The Largesse design problem
abstract: Largesse design is a positive theory of what happens when players in a game, who have a limited willingness to sacrifice for the common good, can coordinate on a welfare-optimal solution. This theory provides an alternative to psychological theories in explaining why players engage in costly punishments and rewards. It also says that players will engage in other low-cost methods of encouraging pro-social behavior, for example, through reputation effects. In this paper, I study the properties and comparative statics of the largesse design problem. Despite a lack of concavity in the maximization problem, solutions are unique and continuous except on a lower-dimensional bifurcation set. In examples, I study these bifurcations, in which a small change in the parameters can lead to a large change in behavior or welfare.

title: The Moderating Role of Nepotism Perception in The Relationship Between Prosocial Behavior and Superego
abstract: This study examines the relationship between superego and prosocial behavior and the moderating role of the perception of nepotism in this relationship. A total of 260 employees from various sectors participated in the study. Using the self-reporting method, participants evaluated their perception of superego, prosocial behavior, and nepotism. According to the findings, a positive relationship was found between the superego levels of the employees and their prosocial behavior levels. At the same time, a negative relationship was found between the prosocial behavior levels of the employees and their perception of nepotism. It also did not play a moderating role in the relationship between nepotism, superego, and prosocial behavior. The findings are discussed in detail in the discussion section, and suggestions for future research are presented. In conclusion, although this study conducted on a limited sample, it contributes to the examination of the test of psychological and social psychological assumptions in an organizational context.

title: Shared decision-making in the treatment of metastatic prostate cancer.
abstract: Treating patients with metastatic prostate cancer is complex as various treatment options are available, each having specific benefits and risks. Health-care providers and patients are often faced with several reasonable options but no clear 'correct' choice. To optimize treatment outcomes, including quality of life and health-care provider and patient satisfaction, patients and care-givers need to engage in the treatment decision-making process. Shared decision-making (SDM) is a process in which the health-care provider, patient, family and/or care-giver are all actively involved in sharing information and building agreement on which treatment or treatments to implement based on preferences and the clinical situation. SDM is recommended by prostate cancer clinical practice guidelines, but implementation varies owing to multiple challenges, including time constraints, logistical concerns and lack of health-care provider comfort in implementing approaches. SDM continues to be explored in the context of localized prostate cancer, but evidence and literature on the importance of SDM in the management of metastatic prostate cancer is scarce. The multidisciplinary health-care team, patients, care-givers, patient advocacy groups, industry, health authorities and other key collaborative partners all have a role in SDM in this disease context. Opportunities to support the initiation and/or further development of effective SDM in clinical practice include targeted clinician training, use of validated decision aids, improved multidisciplinary team support, and increased patient and care-giver involvement.

title: Beyond unison: auditability and partner-differentiated cooperation in joint music-making, with body percussion as a test case
abstract: Interpersonal entrainment is widely held to promote prosocial behavior by dissolving self–other boundaries, yet meta-analytic effects are moderate and shrink markedly when experimenters are blind to the condition. The author proposes a complementary mechanism with a deliberately minimal core: coordinated music-making makes each participant's contribution auditable , generating person-specific information about demonstrated reliability, and this information subsequently produces partner-differentiated cooperation. Auditability differs from generic observability in that contributions are evaluated in real time, within an interdependent task, against a shared standard fixed in advance, namely, meter. The author separates its constitutive conditions (detection and multimodal attribution) from its scope condition (publicity) and from the conditions that make the evidence diagnostic of commitment rather than skill (non-substitutability, visible cost, interference). They argue that the relevant evidence is maintenance of one's part under interference; specify what participants learn that observers cannot; distinguish public availability, mutual recognition, and common knowledge; and give a simple treatment of how reliability estimates converge as group size grows. The two accounts diverge: fusion predicts prosociality undifferentiated within the group, whereas auditability predicts cooperation differentiated by demonstrated reliability. Body percussion is treated as a convenient test case, not as a privileged medium. The author states the core hypothesis, its necessary assumptions, auxiliary and medium-specific hypotheses, and extensions separately and lists which outcomes would falsify the core and which would revise only an extension.

title: A Review of the Philosophical Foundations of Islamic Rules and Ethics in Zurkhaneh Sports Architecture
abstract: Zurkhaneh, the traditional Iranian “house of strength,” represents more than a setting for physical exercise. Its ritual practices integrate bodily training, heroic narratives, music, religious symbolism, hierarchical etiquette, and ethical instruction. This review examines the philosophical and cultural foundations through which Islamic moral values, the tradition of futuwwa or javanmardi (chivalry), Shi’i symbolism, Sufi ethical concepts, and older Iranian traditions have been interpreted within Zurkhaneh sport and architecture. The study adopts a qualitative library-review approach and critically synthesizes historical scholarship, peer-reviewed research, reference works, and cultural-heritage documentation concerning Pahlavani and Zurkhaneh traditions. Particular attention is given to the relationship between ethical instruction and architectural form, including the sunken gowd, the sardam of the morshed, ritual hierarchy, symbolic sporting instruments, poetry, music, and collective practice. The review indicates that Zurkhaneh culture historically linked strength with humility, self-restraint, generosity, loyalty, respect for elders, protection of the vulnerable, and service to the community. These values are closely related to the ethical vocabulary of futuwwa/javanmardi and, in later Iranian contexts, to Shi’i devotion and the exemplary status attributed to Imam Ali. At the same time, the historical origins of the institution remain contested; similarities with older Iranian and Mithraic traditions should therefore be treated as interpretive hypotheses rather than as evidence of an uninterrupted institutional genealogy. Contemporary scholarship likewise shows that Zurkhaneh has evolved substantially over time. The continuing significance of the institution lies not in reproducing a fixed historical form, but in understanding how architecture, ritual, physical training, collective memory, and moral education can operate together. This integrated model provides a useful basis for discussing ethical formation in sport while avoiding romanticized contrasts between traditional and modern athletic practice.
